Weakness in US full-time employment is deepening:

Full-time employment fell-106,000 in July, to 133.55 million, the lowest since December 2024.

This marks the 4th consecutive monthly decline, totaling -1.11 million. 

Since January 2025, full-time employment has dropped by -2.35 million

As a result, the number of full-time workers in the US is now just 1.4% above pre-pandemic levels.

Meanwhile, the full-time employment-to-total employment ratio has fallen to 82.4%, the 3rd-lowest level since March 2018.

US labor market is weak beneath the surface.

US tech is generating record gains for foreign institutional investors:

Norway’s $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, the world’s largest, generated a record +$184.3 billion in profit in H1 2026.

This comes as the fund returned +9.4% over the period, while its 72.1% equity allocation was up +13.0%.

In Q2 2026 alone, the portfolio gained +11.5%, its strongest quarterly performance since Q2 2020.

Equities, primarily driven by AI-related names, led the gains with a +16.0% return during the quarter.

Meanwhile, Nvidia, $NVDA, remained its largest holding at the end of H1 2026, followed by Microsoft, $MSFT, and Apple, $AAPL.

Norway’s fund owns ~1.5% of all publicly listed companies globally and has become one of the world’s largest institutional investors in AI-related companies.

The AI revolution is boosting investment portfolios far beyond America.

For bond investors the choice is always between nominal and real, and as shown in the Real vs. Nominal Yields chart, since 2021 TIPS have outperformed nominals. I expect that to continue as nominals seem too low given where the implied inflation expectations are.

Whether or not the TIPS break-evens carry a market signal (as is commonly assumed) remains an open question for me. Just like the oil futures strip, I’m not sure that break-evens reflect a conscious market opinion or are just a residual of two types of instruments. Case in point: the TIPS chart below shows the TIPS real yield along the horizontal and the break-even along the vertical. I don’t see a pattern between the two.

A significant portion of US corporate software spending is going to waste.

Companies are now spending close to $10,000 per employee per year on software costs in the US.

Meanwhile, ~33% of these software purchases are never used.

At a company with 1,000 employees, unused software alone can represent more than $3 million in annual waste.

As software becomes a larger share of corporate spending, managing these costs is quickly becoming a major source of margin improvement.

Software spending cuts are likely coming soon.

Tech sector breadth is rapidly improving:

75% of S&P 500 technology sector stocks finished above their 200-day moving average last week, the highest percentage since October 2024.

This marked the first time in 219 trading days that this threshold was reached, ending the 9th-longest streak on record.

By comparison, the longest stretch during which fewer than 75% of tech stocks traded above their 200-day moving average lasted 759 trading days, ending on April 22, 2003, following the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

Historically, each time such a streak ended, the technology sector returned +2.5% on average over the following month and +7.3% over the next 3 months.

After 6 months and 12 months, the average gains were +15.5% and +33.4%, respectively.

Meanwhile, 69% of Nasdaq 100 stocks are now trading above their 200-day moving average, near the highest percentage since July 2025.

The tech stock rally is gaining momentum.

I have a confession.

I’ve been building new ways to quantify sentiment data behind the scenes again. I truly can’t help myself, the ideas just keep flowing.

This one is my new favorite.

It’s what I’m calling a “sentiment spread”.

It measures the difference in a specific mood across two different cohorts. In this case we are looking at the conviction levels of MSTR shareholders vs Bitcoiners more broadly.

But there’s a lot going on, so let’s step through it together.

The top section shows both the BTC and MSTR prices over the last few years.

The middle section shows the aggregate conviction levels of Bitcoiners (blue line) and MSTR shareholders (orange line) over the same time duration.

The bottom line combines these and shows the space between them (the spread). So when it’s blue, it shows that Bitcoiners are generally more convicted than MSTR shareholders. When it’s orange, it shows that MSTR shareholders are more convicted than Bitcoiners broadly.

“Ok, cool share dude, but why should I care?”

Because it separates MSTR investor sentiment from the background emotional state of Bitcoin.

If conviction rises across both groups simultaneously, MSTR investors may simply be responding to Bitcoin. But when the two groups diverge, it tells us that something distinct is happening inside the MSTR shareholder community.

That’s exactly what we’re seeing now.

While individual months are noisy, one thing remains true.

Nothing stops this train.

BREAKING: The US Government officially posts its largest July budget deficit in history, at -$432 billion, due to an acceleration in federal spending.

Interest on US debt rose +$26 billion from last July's levels to an alarming $118 billion for the month. 

This puts total interest expense for FY2026 up to $1.17 trillion in FY2026.

As a result, interest expense has officially surpassed both National Defense and Medicare spending.

In other words, the US government now spends more money just on interest than it does to fund the entire US Military or to provide healthcare for seniors.

We cannot afford higher interest rates.
